meta.title: Who really said "It may be the cock that crows, but it is the hen that lays the egg"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Margaret Thatcher really did use this line — twice. But she was quoting a folk proverb that reached print in 1881, and not in these words.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It may be the cock that crows, but it is the hen that lays the egg'?
meta.ogDescription: Thatcher quoted it; she did not coin it. The proverb was collected from African-American folklore and printed in Uncle Remus in 1881.

answer.label: Not Thatcher’s line — a folk proverb she quoted
answer.authorDates: In print by 1881 · collected from the African-American oral tradition
answer.sourceLine: Margaret Thatcher really did use this saying — at a private dinner in 1987, and again in a Washington lecture in September 1991 — but she was quoting, not coining, and neither of her recorded wordings is the one that circulates under her name. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ traces the proverb back through American newspapers to 1881, when Joel Chandler Harris printed it among the “Plantation Proverbs” he collected from the African-American oral tradition.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings
Joel Chandler Harris, 1881 — in the “Plantation Proverbs” section
A private dinner, 1987; the First Clare Boothe Luce Lecture, Washington DC, 23 September 1991
African-American oral tradition; a differently worded precursor recorded from 1659

source.excerpt: Rooster makes mo’ racket dan de hin w’at lay de aig.
trail: We read Project Gutenberg’s full text of Uncle Remus, His Songs and His Sayings ↗ rather than a quotation database, and found the line “Rooster makes mo’ racket dan de hin w’at lay de aig” standing in its Plantation Proverbs list.
Quote Investigator ↗ dates that printing to the 1881 D. Appleton edition, p. 151, and records a differently worded precursor — “The cock crows but the hen goes” — in proverb collections from 1659.

The same page reproduces both Thatcher wordings: “The cocks may crow, but it’s the hen that lays the egg,” which Robert Skidelsky reported hearing at a private dinner in 1987 (Sunday Times, 9 April 1989), and “although the cock may crow, it is the hen that lays the egg,” from her First Clare Boothe Luce Lecture in Washington on 23 September 1991. Neither is the wording in circulation.

We could not read the Thatcher Archive text of the 1991 lecture ourselves — margaretthatcher.org was unreachable from this run — so the 1991 wording rests on Quote Investigator’s transcription and its citation of that archive, not on our own reading of the primary document.
source.excerptNote: Harris printed the proverb in the heavy eye-dialect he used throughout Uncle Remus. In plain English: the rooster makes more racket than the hen that laid the egg.

author.name: Anonymous (African-American folk proverb)
author.heading: About Anonymous (African-American folk proverb)
author.metaLine: In print by 1881 · African-American oral tradition · popularly mis-credited to Margaret Thatcher
author.bio: The saying has no known author. It was collected from the African-American oral tradition of the post-war South and first printed by Joel Chandler Harris in 1881, in the “Plantation Proverbs” that open Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings. It circulated anonymously in American newspapers for the next eighty years before any politician was credited with it.

copyAttribution: It may be the cock that crows, but it is the hen that lays the egg. —an African-American folk proverb in print by 1881, quoted (not coined) by Margaret Thatcher

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The proverb is old, widely travelled, and has been pinned on more than one modern politician.

items.why: She used it — Quote Investigator ↗ documents a 1987 dinner and a 1991 Washington lecture — but the saying was already a century old in print, and her two recorded wordings differ from the version now sold under her name.

Quote Investigator records the Texas governor using a Texan variant at a San Francisco fundraiser in 1992: “As we say in Texas, the rooster may crow, but the hens deliver the goods.” See the chronology ↗.
Harris was the first to print it, in 1881, but he was recording African-American folktales and sayings ↗ rather than inventing them.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who first said it. Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗ is that the saying “can be traced back more than one hundred years to African-American folklore, and precursor sayings existed centuries earlier.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Thatcher used the line as a weapon, not a decoration. In the 1991 Washington lecture she explained that she had made the point “rather brutally” at a dinner given by a British think tank, where, as she put it, politicians counted for little and it was the ideas of intellectuals that were held to rule the world. Paul Johnson, writing in 2007 about a 1980s dinner he attended, describes her delivering it as the tenth speaker and the only woman, after being kept waiting until nearly midnight.
That is a long way from the tidy line about female achievement it has become, and further still from its actual origins in a body of proverbs collected on Southern plantations.
detailsBody: The chain of printings Quote Investigator assembles ↗ runs from Harris’s 1881 “Plantation Proverbs” through American newspapers in 1904, 1907, 1914 and 1916, and turns up in a 1944 Richmond advertisement that oddly labelled it a “new proverb” from wartime England.
Paul Johnson’s 2007 account has the detail only someone in the room would keep: he laughed, long and loud, and then realised he was the only one who found it funny.

Quote Investigator dates the Harris printing to 1881 (D. Appleton, p. 151), gives a 1659 precursor, reproduces Thatcher’s 1987 and 1991 wordings, records Ann Richards’s 1992 variant, and concludes Thatcher used but did not coin the saying.
Joel Chandler Harris was an American journalist and folklorist who wrote down Brer Rabbit stories from the African-American oral tradition.
Uncle Remus is a collection of African American folktales compiled and adapted by Joel Chandler Harris and published in book form in 1881.
Margaret Thatcher (13 October 1925 – 8 April 2013) was a British stateswoman and Prime Minister.
